description: We are a team of university students in engineering, aviation, and medical biophysics.
summary:
In deep space, waiting for symptoms is not a reliable health strategy.

Beyond Earth’s reach, astronauts can’t count on feeling sick to know something is wrong. Slow, silent changes must be caught before they become emergencies.

That is why we built SPECC (Spatial Predictive Environmental Computing Companion): an intelligent health-monitoring and predictive decision-support system designed around one central question.

What if we could identify a health risk before an astronaut even realizes it’s developing?

SPECC is an onboard health companion that warns astronauts before symptoms start. Like a stall horn that alerts a pilot before the aircraft stalls, SPECC predicts how space radiation, altered gravity and immune changes will affect each crew member if exposure continues, then gives a clear treatment plan.

Station sensors gather data on the internal environment while the SPECC robot monitors astronaut health data, running close-up checks such as vitals, personal radiation dose and mood check-ins. A central system computing system combines the information gathered from both, and displays each astronaut’s trend against limits drawn from published NASA sources into a console application. Because the same exposure affects every body differently, each astronaut can view a personalized, color-coded display with plain-language guidance.
details:
What it does and how it works
SPECC (Spatial Predictive Environmental Computing Companion) is an early detection health monitor for long-duration missions. It has three parts. Station sensors measure the environment, such as radiation in each module, air quality and microbes. The SPECC robot measures the person, with close-up checks like vitals, a personal radiation dose, a saliva swab and daily mood and sleep check-ins. A central system combines both, projects each astronaut’s trend forward, and compares it against limits from published NASA sources. The astronaut sees a color-coded personal dashboard showing where each indicator is heading if exposure continues, with a plain-language prevention plan.

We focused on three areas: space radiation, altered gravity (bone, muscle and cardiovascular changes) and immune changes. Where NASA publishes a limit, such as the 600 mSv career radiation dose or keeping bone density at 95% or more of pre-flight, we use it. Where no NASA number exists, as with immune changes, we set our own rule and label it clearly as a team rule. The demo has five screens:

  • Mission Console: each astronaut's status by hazard (OK, Watch, Act now), a "Future you" chart projecting each indicator to landing with and without the plan, a clickable body status map, and a station heatmap of radiation and CO2 by module.
  • Robot Scan: a 3D scene where the SPECC robot drives to the astronaut and runs a vital-sign scan.
  • Station Sensors: a 3D sensor bay showing how station sensors read radiation and CO2.
  • SPECC Bot Simulation: a station map based on real ISS module names, with 11 scripted scenarios: solar storm, skipped workouts, poor sleep and high CO2, daily check-up, cabin CO2 spike, vision change (SANS), rash and shingles risk, isolation and low mood, spacewalk readiness, landing prep, and following the prevention plan.
  • Pitch: our slide deck, including the NASA references

Benefits

  • Warns before symptoms appear, instead of reacting after.
  • Personalized: the same exposure affects each body differently, so each astronaut gets their own prediction based on their profile.
  • Explains every indicator in simple words and says exactly what to do next, so no medical training is assumed.
  • The robot prompts check-ups and countermeasures like exercise as part of the daily routine, and offers companionship against isolation.

Intended impact
SPECC is meant to help crews catch slow, silent changes early and act on their own, while packaging results for the ground team.

Tools and technology
Our demo is an interactive website built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, containing the dashboard, a simulation of the robot and sensors working together, and our pitch deck. We prototyped the central system in Python with Flask, working in VS Code, and published the code on GitHub. All readings in the demo are simulated. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help with research, planning and code.

Creativity
Our idea comes from aviation. Two of our team members are pilots in training, and SPECC works like a stall horn: it sounds before the stall, not after. We paired that with a blood-alcohol-style model, where the same exposure produces a different effect in each person. The friendly companion robot gives the system a face: “your space buddy on board.”

Factors we considered

  • Grounding every threshold in published NASA sources, and being honest about which rules are our own.
  • Why a robot is needed at all: sensors watch the station, SPECC looks after the person.
  • Keeping predictions on a central system so nothing is lost if the robot is charging or broken.
  • Astronauts’ limited time and medical knowledge, so the display is color-coded and the guidance is simple.
  • Mental health as well as physical health, since isolation is one of NASA’s five hazards.
